newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end mixed, late buying boosts market.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end mixed, late buying boosts market.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices ended narrowly mixed Wednesday, after a late day short-covering rally brought bonds off the depressed levels held most of the session.
The 30-year bond fell an 1/8 of a point to 100-20/32, while its yield was unchanged at 6.45 percent -- holding at its lowest level since early March.
But most of the day's action took place at the short end, primarily the two-year note, which had nearly $7.1 billion in trading volume, according to GovPx.

Maureen Mooney, senior fixed income specialist at GovPx, noted that trading in the short end was 50 percent higher than normal, while overall trading volume was 33 percent above a typical Wednesday. The two-year note was up 1/32 on the day.
The market traditionally trades light on days of a Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting, but with virtually no one expecting a rate move, the FOMC meeting went largely unnoticed.
"Since nobody expected a move, the (no action) announcement had no impact," said Michelle Colley Laughlin, chief Treasury market analyst at Prudential Securities Inc.

Ahead of the 1415 EST/1915 GMT announcement that the Federal Reserve left rates unchanged, the bond was down about a 1/2 of a point, but those losses were quickly reversed as the dollar started to rise.
The dollar was boosted by Treasury Undersecretary Jeffrey Shafer's mid-afternoon remarks reiterating the Clinton administration's committment to a "strong" dollar.

The U.S. currency was at 1.5070 German marks late Wednesday, above its opening quote near 1.5052 marks. Aiding bonds was Bundesbank council member Reimut Jochimsen's comment that there is more room for the dollar to appreciate.
"I don't see room for much going down in the dollar, but more for going up of the dollar," Jochimsen said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television.
Bond players suggested that a strong dollar would continue to encourage foreign buyers of Treasuries.
One head trader at a Japanese-owned primary dealership concurred, adding that helping the late rally was the expectation for Treasuries traded overseas to be well bid on Thursday.
"The market has a tendency to trade up late in the day because of hopes of Japanese buying at night," he said.

Treasury prices rose early in the U.S. session, as the market shrugged off a 0.4 percent rise in the overall producer price index for October, rather focusing on the 0.3 percent drop in the "core" PPI, which excludes food and energy prices.

Some also cited the anticipation of an outright purchase of coupons -- a coupon pass -- by the Fed as helping the market early in the session. However, analysts moved their forecast of a coupon pass to next week.
A bout of profit-taking ensued, sending Treasuries lower, with rumors of a pension fund selling bonds and buying twos leading the way.
"There were more shorts out there then we thought," said Mead Briggs, director of government proprietary trading at CS First Boston Corp.
He added that once the market began to reverse losses in the afternoon, many sellers rushed to cover those shorts.
The market's near-term performance depends on the retail sales report for October, due Thursday at 0830 EST/1330 EST, players said.
Both overall retail sales and sales excluding autos are expected to show a rise of 0.3 percent, according to a Reuters poll. October consumer prices will be released simultaneously.

The overall CPI is seen moving up 0.3 percent, while the core CPI is expected to show a 0.2 percent rise. "Unless CPI has a 'four' in it, the real important numbers are retail sales," Briggs said, referring to a rise of 0.4 percent.

"The (consumer) demand side is the focus," he added. "If the demand side of the economy does well, current (bond) levels are expensive, but if demand slows down, they're not expensive because the market may start chattering about a Fed ease."
Laughlin, though, cautions that October retail sales rarely correlate to holiday spending patterns.

Meanwhile, the three-month Treasury bill rate was unchanged at 5.03 percent, while the six-month bill rate was also unchanged at 5.07 percent. The year bill rate fell two basis points to 5.41 percent.

With the two-year note outperforming the rest of the curve, players said two-year notes are attractive since the yield curve has begun to flatten. "Twos are expensive to (Fed) funds, but to the rest of the curve, they are cheap," Laughlin said.
-- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867
